review.summary:
### 🎯 A lock timeout on the ledger lost the capture outright

When the ledger was slow to answer, `capturePayment` threw, the webhook handler let the error out, and Stripe got a 500. The order stayed unpaid until somebody noticed and replayed the event by hand. The PR description counts four of those last month.

### 🔧 Retry in-process instead of handing the failure back to Stripe

A new `withBackoff` helper runs a task up to five times, sleeping a jittered exponential delay between attempts (500ms base, so roughly 0-0.5s, 0-1s, 0-2s, 0-4s). `handleWebhook` now runs `dispatch` through it rather than calling it directly, so a lock timeout is retried inside the same request instead of waiting an hour for Stripe's next delivery.

### 🔍 Details

The jitter is full jitter — `Math.random() * base * 2 ** (attempt - 1)` — not the exponential value itself, so a burst of simultaneous failures spreads out instead of retrying in lockstep. Exhausting the attempts throws `RetriesExhausted`, which carries the task name, the attempt count and the original error. The handler catches that one class and returns; anything else still propagates.

The two new tests pin the retry-then-succeed path (two calls to `capturePayment`) and the give-up path (five calls, handler resolves).

### ⚠️ Worth knowing

The retry re-enters the charge path with nothing keyed to the Stripe event, so a redelivery can capture the same payment twice. The give-up branch makes that more likely rather than less, because it returns 200 and tells Stripe the delivery succeeded. Both are in the comments.

chapters.title: The webhook handler runs through it
chapters.explanation: `handleWebhook` now calls `dispatch` via the helper, and swallows `RetriesExhausted` so Stripe sees a 200. This is where the risk lives: the existing `inFlight` guard is keyed on the payment intent, and the retry loop re-enters the charge path.

chapters.title: What the new tests pin down
chapters.explanation: Two cases: a capture that fails once and then succeeds, and one that never succeeds. Both assert on how many times `capturePayment` was called, which is the right thing to assert here.

comments.body:
A redelivered webhook can capture the same payment twice.

`inFlight` is keyed on the payment intent and cleared in the `finally`, so it only ever guards two deliveries that overlap in time. Nothing records the Stripe event id, and `capturePayment` takes no idempotency key — so when Stripe redelivers `payment_intent.requires_capture`, this line walks straight back into the charge path and the customer pays twice.

Stripe retries a delivery for up to three days, and the give-up branch below returns 200, which is exactly when a redelivery arrives. Key the guard on `event.id` and pass it to `capturePayment` as the idempotency key.

Giving up returns 200, so Stripe stops redelivering and the payment is lost for good.

That is the bug this PR exists to fix, moved one layer along: before, a failure at least came back an hour later. Now five attempts inside one request is the whole budget. Rethrow after the retries, or write the event somewhere a human reads, so a ledger outage longer than two seconds doesn't quietly drop orders.

`name` holds a payment intent id, which makes the retry logs read oddly.

The only call site passes `webhook:pi_3Px…`, so the warnings come out as `task: "webhook:pi_3Px…"`. `key` would say what it actually is.

verdict.reasoning:
The retry path can charge a customer twice — that is the blocker, and everything else here is fine.

- **Traced the dedupe guard** — `inFlight` is an in-process `Set` keyed on `event.data.object.id` and cleared in the `finally`, so it survives exactly as long as the request. Nothing in the diff records a Stripe event id anywhere.
- **Followed the redelivery** — the give-up branch returns 200, so Stripe marks the delivery done; but its own retries also fire on any 5xx or timeout, and each one re-enters `dispatch` through this line with no idempotency key.
- **Read the backoff maths** — full jitter, base 500ms, five attempts. Worst case is about 7.5s held open in one request, which is survivable, and the jitter does spread a thundering herd.
- **Checked the tests** — they pin the two paths the description claims and assert on call counts. Neither covers a second delivery of the same event, which is the case that breaks.
- **Didn't run anything** — this was reviewed from the diff alone, with no checkout. `capturePayment` is not in the diff, so "takes no idempotency key" comes from the call site; if it derives one internally from the intent, the blocker softens to a minor. Worth confirming in `src/payments/capture.ts`.
